note: PSLE Science process skills. Three drill types: variables (name what was changed, measured and kept the same), fairtest (find the flaw and fix it), readdata (say which comparison supports a conclusion).

items.setup: Four identical dishes each hold 50 ml of water. Each dish is placed in a room at a different temperature. After three hours, the volume of water remaining in each dish is measured.
items.aim: To find out how temperature affects the rate of evaporation.
items.measured: The volume of water remaining after three hours
keptSame: The size and shape of the dish
items.teachingPoint: Only one thing may be changed on purpose. Everything else that could affect the result must be kept the same, or you cannot tell which factor caused the change.

items.setup: A wooden block is pulled across four surfaces, glass, wood, carpet and sandpaper, using a spring balance. The same block is used each time and the force needed to keep it moving is recorded.
items.aim: To find out how the type of surface affects the frictional force.
items.measured: The force shown on the spring balance
keptSame: The speed at which the block is pulled
distractors: The type of spring balance readings
items.teachingPoint: The thing you measure is never the thing you keep the same. If frictional force is what you are investigating, it belongs in the measured box, not the kept-the-same box.

items.setup: Five sets of ten identical seeds are placed on cotton wool. Each set is given a different volume of water each day. All sets are kept in the same warm, lit room. After one week the number of seeds that have germinated in each set is counted.
items.aim: To find out how the amount of water affects germination.
items.changed: The volume of water given each day
items.measured: The number of seeds that germinate
keptSame: The number of seeds in each set
distractors: The day the seeds were planted
The colour of the cotton wool
items.teachingPoint: Watch for the trap of listing the changed variable among the things kept the same. Read your own answer back: the changed one appears exactly once.

items.setup: Rods of copper, iron, glass and plastic, all the same length and thickness, are each held in hot water at 90 degrees Celsius. A small blob of wax is fixed to the far end of each rod. The time taken for each blob of wax to melt is recorded.
items.aim: To find out which material is the best conductor of heat.
items.changed: The material the rod is made of
items.measured: The time taken for the wax to melt
keptSame: The length and thickness of the rod
The temperature of the hot water
The size of the blob of wax
items.teachingPoint: When time is what you record, the measurement is a number of seconds. An answer such as which wax melts is an observation, not a measurement.

items.setup: An electromagnet is made by winding wire around an iron nail. The number of turns of wire is varied while the same battery is used each time. The number of paper clips picked up is counted.
items.aim: To find out how the number of turns of wire affects the strength of the electromagnet.
items.changed: The number of turns of wire
items.measured: The number of paper clips picked up
distractors: The number of turns of wire
The size of the paper clips box
items.teachingPoint: The number of paper clips is a way of measuring the strength. Strength itself is what the experiment is about; the paper clips are how you put a number on it.

items.setup: Four identical potted plants are placed at different distances from a lamp. All receive the same amount of water and are kept at the same temperature. After a week, a leaf from each is tested for starch.
items.aim: To find out how the amount of light affects photosynthesis.
items.changed: The distance of the plant from the lamp
items.measured: The amount of starch found in the leaf
keptSame: The type and size of plant
distractors: The brightness of the lamp over time
items.teachingPoint: Distance from the lamp is the practical way of changing the amount of light. Naming the thing you physically adjusted is what the examiner wants.

items.setup: Four leafy shoots of the same plant are placed in identical tubes of water. Each is given a different number of leaves. All four are left in the same room for three hours, then the volume of water lost from each tube is measured.
items.aim: To find out how the number of leaves affects the rate of water loss.
items.changed: The number of leaves on the shoot
items.measured: The volume of water lost from the tube
keptSame: The temperature and air movement in the room
items.teachingPoint: Air movement is easy to forget among the things kept the same, but a fan blowing on only one tube would ruin the experiment. Ask what else could change the result.

items.setup: Equal masses of sugar are added to five beakers, each containing 200 ml of water at a different temperature. Each mixture is stirred at the same rate and the time taken for the sugar to dissolve completely is recorded.
items.aim: To find out how temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves.
items.measured: The time taken for the sugar to dissolve completely
items.teachingPoint: Stirring rate belongs in the kept-the-same list. Anything a person does differently between setups is a variable, even when it is not equipment.

items.setup: A student wants to find out whether wind speed affects how fast water evaporates. She puts 50 ml of water in a shallow dish beside a fan, and 30 ml of water in a tall narrow jar in a still corner. After two hours she compares how much water is left.
flawOptions: Two things were changed at once: the air movement and the container, and the starting volumes differ
She did not leave them for long enough
She should have used hot water in both
There is nothing wrong with this experiment
items.fix: Use two identical dishes, each with the same volume of water, and change only whether the fan is on. Then any difference in water lost can only be due to the air movement.
items.teachingPoint: When two things change at once, the result cannot tell you which one caused it. This is the single most common flaw in a PSLE fair test question.

items.setup: A student tests three materials to see which keeps a drink warmest. He wraps a large mug in wool, a small mug in cotton and a large mug in foil, fills each with hot water from the same kettle, and measures the temperature after 20 minutes.
flawOptions: The mugs are not all the same size, so the amount of water and surface area differ
He should have used cold water instead
Twenty minutes is too short a time
He should have measured the temperature at the start only
items.fix: Use three identical mugs with the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, changing only the wrapping material.
items.teachingPoint: Identical containers are almost always required. A different size changes both the volume of liquid and the surface area losing heat, so two variables move at once.

items.setup: A student wants to find out whether seeds need water to germinate. She puts ten seeds on damp cotton wool in a warm cupboard, and ten seeds on dry cotton wool on a cold windowsill. After a week only the damp set has germinated.
flawOptions: Temperature was changed as well as water, so the result could be due to either
Ten seeds is not enough to test
She should have used a different type of seed in each set
Seeds do not need water, so the aim is wrong
items.fix: Keep both sets in the same warm cupboard, changing only whether the cotton wool is damp or dry.
items.teachingPoint: The conclusion is probably right, but the experiment cannot prove it. An experiment that reaches the correct answer by an unfair method still scores no marks.

items.setup: A student tests which shoe grips best. He pulls one shoe across a tiled floor and another across a rubber mat, using a spring balance, and records the force needed for each.
flawOptions: The surfaces are different, so he is testing the surface rather than the shoe
He should have used a heavier spring balance
The shoes should have been new
He should have pulled faster
items.fix: Pull both shoes across the same surface, changing only which shoe is being tested. The masses inside the shoes should also be made equal.
items.teachingPoint: Ask what the aim actually names. The aim is about shoes, so the shoe is what should change and the surface is what should stay the same.

items.setup: A student times how long a toy car takes to roll down a ramp. She releases it once from the top, records 2.4 seconds, and concludes that the car always takes 2.4 seconds.
flawOptions: She took only one reading, so she cannot know whether it was a reliable result
She should have used a longer ramp
The car should have been pushed rather than released
There is nothing wrong with this experiment
items.fix: Repeat the run several times from the same starting point and calculate the average, so that a single unusual reading does not mislead.
items.teachingPoint: Repeating and averaging is about reliability rather than fairness. A question asking how to improve an experiment very often wants the word repeat.

items.setup: A student investigates whether stirring makes sugar dissolve faster. He stirs a beaker of warm water with sugar and leaves an unstirred beaker of cold water with sugar. The stirred one dissolves first.
flawOptions: The water temperature was different as well as the stirring
He should have used more sugar
Sugar does not dissolve in cold water at all
He should have stirred both beakers
items.fix: Use water at the same temperature in both beakers, changing only whether the mixture is stirred.
items.teachingPoint: Whenever a setup names two differences, one of them is the flaw. Underline every difference between the two setups before answering.

items.setup: A student tests whether a new fertiliser helps plants grow. She gives fertiliser to one plant on a sunny windowsill and no fertiliser to another plant in a shaded corner, and measures their heights after two weeks.
flawOptions: The amount of light was different, so the result could be due to light rather than fertiliser
Two weeks is not long enough for plants to grow
She should have used fertiliser on both plants
Height is the wrong thing to measure
items.fix: Place both plants in the same position with the same light and water, changing only whether fertiliser is given.
items.teachingPoint: A setup with no untreated comparison, or with a comparison that differs in another way, cannot support any conclusion about the treatment.

items.setup: A student wants to show that saliva breaks down starch. She adds saliva to a tube of starch solution, leaves it, then tests it and finds no starch. She concludes that saliva broke down the starch.
flawOptions: There is no control tube without saliva, so she cannot know the saliva caused it
She should have tested for sugar instead
She should have used more starch solution
Saliva does not break down starch
items.fix: Set up a second identical tube with water instead of saliva, kept at the same temperature for the same time. If starch remains in that tube but not in the saliva tube, the saliva caused the change.
items.teachingPoint: A control is the setup where the thing being tested is absent. Without it, you cannot rule out that the change would have happened anyway.

items.setup: Four sets of identical seeds were kept for one week in different conditions.
items.table:
Set 1  moist, warm, in light      germinated
Set 2  dry,   warm, in light      did not germinate
Set 3  moist, warm, in darkness   germinated
Set 4  moist, cold, in light      did not germinate
items.question: Which two sets should be compared to show that seeds need water to germinate?
items.teachingPoint: Compare the pair that differs in one factor only. Sets 1 and 2 differ only in water, so any difference in the result must be caused by the water.

items.setup: The same four sets of seeds.
items.table:
Set 1  moist, warm, in light      germinated
Set 2  dry,   warm, in light      did not germinate
Set 3  moist, warm, in darkness   germinated
Set 4  moist, cold, in light      did not germinate
items.question: What does Set 3 show?
options: Light is not needed for germination
Warmth is not needed for germination
items.teachingPoint: Set 3 germinated with no light, which rules light out. Every row in a table is there for a reason; the ones that seem to contradict your expectation are usually the most important.

items.setup: Four identical wet cloths were left to dry and the time taken was recorded.
items.table:
Cloth W  shaded, still air   300 minutes
Cloth X  shaded, windy       180 minutes
Cloth Y  sunny,  still air   140 minutes
Cloth Z  sunny,  windy        80 minutes
items.question: Which two cloths should be compared to show that moving air increases the rate of evaporation?
items.teachingPoint: W and X are both shaded, so only the air movement differs. Comparing W and Z would change two things at once and prove nothing about either.

items.setup: Identical cups of hot water at 80 degrees Celsius were wrapped in different materials and the temperature was measured after 20 minutes.
items.table:
Wool       62 degrees Celsius
Cotton     55 degrees Celsius
Foil       41 degrees Celsius
No wrap    38 degrees Celsius
items.question: Which conclusion do these results support?
options: Wool is the poorest conductor of heat of the materials tested
Foil is the best material for keeping water warm
items.teachingPoint: The smallest temperature drop means the least heat was transferred to the surroundings, which makes that material the poorest conductor. No material makes anything hotter.

items.setup: Numbers of an insect and of the birds that eat them were counted over four years.
items.table:
Year 1   8000 insects   120 birds
Year 2   3000 insects   130 birds
Year 3   2000 insects    70 birds
Year 4   6000 insects    50 birds
items.question: Which statement best describes the pattern in this data?
options: A fall in the insect numbers is followed by a fall in the bird numbers
The insect and bird numbers always rise and fall together
The birds have no effect on the insect numbers
The insect numbers fall every year
items.teachingPoint: The predator responds after the prey, not at the same time. The word followed is what turns a description of two columns into a statement about cause.

items.setup: Leafy shoots in identical tubes of water were left for three hours and the water lost was measured.
items.table:
Shoot 1  all leaves,      still air   12 ml
Shoot 2  all leaves,      fan on      21 ml
Shoot 3  half the leaves, still air    7 ml
Shoot 4  no leaves,       still air    1 ml
items.question: Which comparison shows that water is lost mainly through the leaves?
items.teachingPoint: Shoots 1, 3 and 4 differ only in the number of leaves, and the water lost falls as leaves are removed. Shoot 4 still lost 1 ml, so a little is lost elsewhere; noticing that detail marks a careful answer.

items.setup: An electromagnet was tested and the number of paper clips it picked up was recorded.
items.table:
1 battery,  20 turns   4 clips
1 battery,  40 turns   8 clips
2 batteries, 20 turns  9 clips
items.question: What do these results show?
options: Both more turns of wire and more batteries increase the strength
Only the number of turns affects the strength
Only the number of batteries affects the strength
The strength does not depend on either factor
items.teachingPoint: Two separate comparisons are available here, each holding one factor steady. Use both rather than reading the table as a single list.

items.setup: Four potted plants were kept for a week and their leaves tested for starch.
items.table:
Plant 1  light, watered,     normal air              starch present
Plant 2  dark,  watered,     normal air              no starch
Plant 3  light, watered,     carbon dioxide removed  no starch
Plant 4  light, not watered, normal air              no starch
items.question: Which two plants should be compared to show that carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis?
items.teachingPoint: Plants 1 and 3 differ only in the carbon dioxide. In a four-row table like this, each row is designed to isolate one factor against row 1.
